rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec quarter-point hike ~89%, half-point priced out (CME FedWatch via Reuters, Nov 23); ECB Dec ~90%; BoE Dec ~80%; BoJ Dec ~84%; BoC Dec ~44%; RBA 4.85%
rows.read: A December Fed hike is still expected, but bets on a bigger half-point move vanished after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned against hiking too far. The European Central Bank and Bank of England are also expected to hike, while Australia's weakening economy makes another Reserve Bank of Australia hike unlikely. US rates still look set to rise further than most, which keeps supporting the dollar.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: Australia flash composite PMI Nov 46.1 (Oct 48.2); NZ Q3 retail sales volume +2.2% q/q (fcst 0.5%); Australia jobs Oct −43.5K
rows.read: Australian business activity is shrinking at its fastest pace in more than five years, another blow to the Aussie. New Zealand shoppers, by contrast, spent far more than expected over the summer quarter, which helps the kiwi. Euro-area, UK and US business surveys for November come out on Monday.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: US core PCE Oct due Wed (fcst +0.3% m/m, 3.2% y/y); UK CPI Oct 3.6%, core 2.8%; euro-area CPI Oct 4.0%; Australia CPI Oct due Tue (fcst 4.8% y/y)
rows.read: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. Australian firms say price rises are slowing, which eases pressure on their central bank. Wednesday's US core inflation figures are the big test for the Fed this week.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: US stock futures ~+2% in Asia (Al Jazeera, Nov 23); Kospi down as much as 5.8%; S&P 500 −3.7% Friday, >10% below its record; USD/JPY +0.3%
rows.read: US stock futures bounced overnight after last week's AI-driven slide, which cooled demand for the yen and the franc. Asian shares still fell, and Asian governments stepped in to steady their markets. Weekend threats in the Gulf, including reported mines near the Strait of Hormuz, keep some caution in place.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent ~$92.3–92.7, WTI ~$83.3–83.6 in Asia (Reuters, FinanceFeeds); gold ~$3,627, about +3% from Friday's close (GoldPrice.com via Hercules)
rows.read: Oil held steady overnight as markets waited to see whether Gulf threats turn into lost supply, which leaves the Canadian dollar without fresh support. Gold bounced back strongly, which helps the Aussie. Energy buyers such as Japan and the euro area still benefit from oil well below this year's highs.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: Hedge funds (CFTC, Nov 17): USD index −1.3K (flipped short), EUR −76.6K, GBP +28.8K, JPY −23.8K, CHF −19.8K, CAD −72.1K, AUD +38.0K, NZD −23.6K; asset managers GBP −104.6K, AUD −182.7K, EUR +147.2K
rows.read: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar after betting on it, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: US 10-year ~4.92% (−21bp on the week); ECB Financial Stability Review: France debt 119% of GDP, deficit 5.5%
rows.read: France's debts, flagged by the European Central Bank as a risk, keep weighing on the euro. Record US government borrowing still keeps long-term US borrowing costs high, though they slipped below 5% as money rushed into bonds during last week's stock slide.
